name: Oxabolone

angle.text: Oxabolone is a nandrolone-family anabolic steroid that appears in muscle-building discussions as one of the obscure compounds in that class, with users associating it with lean mass gain. Almost nothing is published on it, so its use for physique rests on its chemical family and anecdote.

summary: An obscure nandrolone-family anabolic steroid that was never marketed itself and is banned in sport, with almost no published research.
note: Prohibited by WADA; one case report links it to mucosal hyperpigmentation.
currentQuick:
Oxabolone is an anabolic steroid related to nandrolone. The parent compound was never sold as a drug, though an injectable ester called oxabolone cipionate has been used medically.
Very little has been published about it. No trials of its effects on muscle or appearance were found.
How it works: As an anabolic-androgenic steroid it is classed as an androgen receptor agonist, but encyclopedic sources give no details of its potency or metabolism.
Risks and caveats: It is on the WADA prohibited list. A 1995 case report described mucosal hyperpigmentation associated with it; no broader safety data were found.
deepLead:
Oxabolone (also called 4-hydroxy-19-nortestosterone) is a synthetic anabolic-androgenic steroid in the nandrolone (19-nortestosterone) group. The parent compound was never marketed as a drug; its cipionate ester, oxabolone cipionate, is the form that has seen medical use, given by intramuscular injection.
It appears on the World Anti-Doping Agency's list of prohibited substances and is therefore banned in most major sports. Published literature on the compound is sparse. No clinical trials of its muscle-building or appearance effects were found; the only indexed human report concerns a skin and mucosal side effect.

name: SM-130686

angle.text: SM-130686 is an oral growth hormone secretagogue that gets mentioned in muscle and anti-aging circles because raising growth hormone is linked to leaner, fuller-looking physiques. It is known from lab and animal papers; its muscle or appearance effects in people are untested.

summary: An experimental oral oxindole growth hormone secretagogue known from lab and animal papers, with no human trials of muscle or appearance effects.
note: Not an approved medicine; no human efficacy or safety trials were found.
currentQuick:
SM-130686 is a research compound that stimulates growth hormone release by activating the ghrelin receptor. Unlike peptide secretagogues it is a small molecule designed to work by mouth.
The literature is mostly chemistry and animal or cell-based pharmacology from the 2000s. No human trials were found.
How it works: It binds and activates the ghrelin (growth hormone secretagogue) receptor, which triggers growth hormone release from pituitary cells in laboratory studies.
Risks and caveats: Human safety has not been published. The compound is experimental, and analytical methods exist for detecting secretagogues in urine for doping control.
deepLead:
SM-130686 is an experimental, orally active, non-peptide growth hormone secretagogue built on an oxindole scaffold. It was characterised in the early 2000s as a ghrelin receptor agonist that stimulates growth hormone release.
Published work consists of medicinal chemistry, laboratory pharmacology, animal studies and analytical methods for doping control. No human efficacy trials were found, and the compound is not an approved medicine.

name: Bezafibrate

angle.text: Bezafibrate is a lipid-lowering drug that comes up in fat-loss forums because it acts on the same PPAR-delta pathway as compounds like GW501516, so some posters treat it as a related fat-burning option. Its use for body composition is untested and based on that association.

summary: A prescription fibrate and pan-PPAR agonist for blood lipids, discussed in fat-loss circles only by association with PPAR-delta compounds.
note: Established lipid drug; no studies of body-composition or appearance effects were found.
currentQuick:
Bezafibrate is a long-established prescription drug for high triglycerides and mixed cholesterol problems. It activates PPAR receptors, which is why it comes up alongside PPAR-delta compounds in fat-loss conversations.
Its trial record is in cardiovascular disease, dyslipidemia and the liver condition primary biliary cholangitis. No trials of fat loss or appearance outcomes were found.
How it works: It activates PPAR-alpha mainly, with some activity at PPAR-gamma and PPAR-delta, increasing triglyceride breakdown and altering HDL metabolism.
Risks and caveats: Reported effects include abnormal liver enzymes, muscle problems (rarely severe) and gastrointestinal upset. Sources list it as contraindicated in severe liver or kidney impairment, gallstone disease and pregnancy. It is prescription-only.
deepLead:
Bezafibrate is an oral fibrate lipid-lowering drug sold under brand names such as Bezalip. It lowers LDL cholesterol and triglycerides and raises HDL cholesterol, and it is described as a pan-agonist of the peroxisome proliferator-activated receptors (PPARs), acting on alpha, gamma and delta subtypes.
It is a prescription medicine, used mainly in dyslipidemia and, off the main labelled indication, studied in primary biliary cholangitis (PBC). It is mentioned in looksmaxxing and fat-loss discussions mainly as a PPAR agonist related to PPAR-delta compounds, though its documented uses are medical.

name: Seladelpar

angle.text: Seladelpar is an approved PPAR-delta agonist for a liver condition. Fat-loss circles discuss it only because it shares a target with GW501516, which is promoted for endurance and leanness. Its use for body composition is untested; the approved studies concern liver disease.

summary: An FDA-approved PPAR-delta agonist for primary biliary cholangitis; its fat-loss relevance comes only from sharing a target with GW501516.
note: Prescription liver drug under accelerated approval; no studies of appearance or body composition.
currentQuick:
Seladelpar is a prescription PPAR-delta agonist approved in the US in 2024 for primary biliary cholangitis, a chronic liver disease. It sits in this wiki because it hits the same receptor as GW501516-type research compounds.
Its trials measure liver markers and itch, not fat loss or looks.
How it works: It activates PPAR-delta, which reduces bile acid synthesis in liver cells; the label says the precise mechanism in PBC is not well understood.
Risks and caveats: Reported adverse reactions include headache, abdominal pain, nausea, abdominal distension and dizziness. The label warns about fractures, liver test abnormalities and biliary obstruction. It is available by prescription only.
deepLead:
Seladelpar (brand name Livdelzi; research codes MBX-8025 and RWJ-800025) is an oral, selective peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor delta (PPAR-delta) agonist. The US FDA approved it in August 2024 for primary biliary cholangitis (PBC), together with ursodeoxycholic acid in adults with an inadequate response to it, or alone in those who cannot tolerate it.
The approval was accelerated, based on reduction of alkaline phosphatase; the label states that improved survival or prevention of liver decompensation has not been demonstrated. The drug is discussed in fat-loss and PPAR-delta contexts because it shares a target with research compounds such as GW501516, but its studied use is in liver disease, and no studies of appearance or body-composition outcomes were found.

name: Elafibranor

angle.text: Elafibranor is an approved dual PPAR-alpha/delta agonist for a liver condition. It is mentioned in fat-loss discussion because PPAR-delta activation is linked to greater fat burning, though its appearance or fat-loss effects have not been studied.

summary: An approved dual PPAR-alpha/delta agonist for primary biliary cholangitis, with no research on appearance or fat-loss outcomes.
note: Prescription liver drug under accelerated approval; NASH phase 3 trial was terminated.
currentQuick:
Elafibranor is a prescription drug approved in 2024 for primary biliary cholangitis. It activates two PPAR receptors, including PPAR-delta, which links it to fat-metabolism discussions.
Its trials track liver markers; none examine body composition or looks.
How it works: It and its main metabolite activate PPAR-alpha and PPAR-delta (and PPAR-gamma in vitro), receptors that regulate fat and bile acid metabolism.
Risks and caveats: Reported reactions include weight gain, diarrhea, abdominal pain, nausea, joint pain, muscle injury and fracture, among others. It is prescription-only.
deepLead:
Elafibranor (brand name Iqirvo; also GFT505) is an oral dual PPAR-alpha and PPAR-delta agonist developed by Genfit and marketed by Ipsen for primary biliary cholangitis (PBC). The US FDA granted accelerated approval in June 2024, and the EU granted conditional authorization in September 2024.
It is indicated with ursodeoxycholic acid in adults with an inadequate response, or alone in those who cannot tolerate it. It had earlier been developed for nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH), where a large phase 3 trial was terminated. No studies of cosmetic, fat-loss or muscle outcomes were found; its relevance here is as a PPAR-delta-acting drug.

name: GW0742

angle.text: GW0742 is a research PPAR-delta agonist sold gray-market as a "Cardarine 2.0", and users take it in cutting phases hoping for greater fat burning and endurance. The evidence for that use is lab and animal data; human physique trials have not been run.

summary: A GSK PPAR-delta research compound sold gray-market as "Cardarine 2.0", with lab and animal data only and no human trials.
note: Not approved; analogue GW501516 promoted tumour growth in rodent studies and long-term human safety is unknown.
currentQuick:
GW0742 is a selective PPAR-delta agonist made by GlaxoSmithKline and used mostly as a lab tool. Some bodybuilding and fat-loss communities market it as a stronger sibling of GW501516.
Published research is cell and animal work on inflammation, metabolism and the heart; no human trials were found.
How it works: It activates PPAR-delta, a nuclear receptor involved in fatty acid oxidation, glucose handling and inflammation, in laboratory models.
Risks and caveats: It is not an approved medicine and human safety data are lacking. Rodent studies of the related GW501516 reported tumour promotion, and that concern is cited for GW0742 as well.
deepLead:
GW0742 (also GW610742 and proposed trade name fitorine) is an investigational PPAR-delta (PPAR-beta/delta) agonist investigated by GlaxoSmithKline and used widely as a laboratory tool compound. It is not an approved medicine.
Grokipedia reports that it is sold illicitly to bodybuilders and athletes under names such as "Cardarine 2.0", positioned as an alternative to the related compound GW501516; it also notes concerns, drawn from rodent work on its analogue, about tumour promotion. No human clinical trials were found.

name: L-165041

angle.text: L-165041 is a lab PPAR-delta agonist that appears in fat-loss and endurance discussions as another member of the GW501516 family, with users linking the pathway to greater fat burning and leanness. Evidence comes from cell and mouse studies; human fat-loss data are lacking.

summary: A lab PPAR-delta agonist used in cell and mouse studies; no human fat-loss data exist.
note: Research chemical with no human studies.
currentQuick:
L-165041 is a laboratory compound that switches on PPAR-delta, a receptor that helps control how cells handle fats.
It has been used in cell and rodent experiments on metabolism, heart, vessel and nerve biology. It has not been tested in people for fat loss.
How it works: It binds PPAR-delta, which regulates genes involved in fatty acid metabolism.
Risks and caveats: No human safety data exist. It is a research chemical and not an approved medicine.
deepLead:
L-165041 is a research chemical that selectively activates PPAR-delta (PPARbeta/delta), a nuclear receptor involved in the regulation of fatty acid metabolism. It is used in laboratory studies of lipid metabolism, heart, blood vessel and nerve cell biology, and is listed by chemical suppliers as a research tool.
Published work consists of cell-culture and animal experiments. In insulin-resistant db/db mice, treatment with L-165041 altered lipid metabolism, and in cultured rat heart cells it reduced hypertrophic responses. No published human study has tested it for fat loss or any appearance-related purpose.
It appears in fat-loss discussions as a compound in the same pathway as better-known PPAR-delta agonists studied as exercise mimetics.

name: Acadesine

angle.text: Acadesine (AICAR) is promoted in fat-loss and performance circles as an exercise mimetic, with users hoping for greater fat burning without extra training. The idea comes from a 2008 mouse study; human fat-loss effects have not been shown.

summary: AMPK activator hyped as an exercise mimetic; no human fat-loss evidence, and banned in sport.
note: WADA-prohibited; no human appearance data.
currentQuick:
Acadesine (AICAR) is a compound that activates AMPK, a cellular energy sensor. A 2008 mouse study reported endurance gains, and it is sold online as an exercise mimetic.
It was tested in humans for heart-surgery protection, not fat loss, and that trial stopped for futility.
How it works: It is converted inside cells to an AMP-like molecule that activates AMPK, raising fat oxidation and glucose uptake in muscle in animal studies.
Risks and caveats: It is not approved, and is on the WADA prohibited list. Human safety data for body-composition use are lacking.
deepLead:
Acadesine, also called AICAR or AICA riboside, is a nucleoside that activates AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK), an enzyme that senses cellular energy status. It was studied clinically for protecting the heart during surgery and in some blood cancers, and in 2008 a mouse study described it as an exercise mimetic, which led to interest from athletes and in online fat-loss and performance discussions.
Human data for appearance or body-composition purposes are absent. The World Anti-Doping Agency has listed acadesine as a prohibited substance since 2009.

name: SLU-PP-332

angle.text: SLU-PP-332 is billed in fat-loss circles as an exercise mimetic that could deliver leanness and endurance gains without extra training. The basis is mouse research showing exercise-like gene activity and less fat gain; human data do not exist.

summary: Mouse-tested ERR agonist billed as an exercise mimetic; no human data exist.
note: Preclinical only; detectable by anti-doping labs.
currentQuick:
SLU-PP-332 is an experimental compound that activates estrogen-related receptors and, in mice, produced an exercise-like response and better running capacity.
Studies are limited to mice and cells, and no human results are published.
How it works: It activates ERR alpha, beta and gamma, receptors that control mitochondrial and fat metabolism in muscle.
Risks and caveats: Human safety is unknown. It is not an approved drug, and doping-control methods for it have been published.
deepLead:
SLU-PP-332 is an experimental synthetic agonist of the estrogen-related receptors (ERR alpha, beta and gamma), described by its developers as an exercise mimetic because it triggered an exercise-like gene program and increased running capacity in mice.
Published results come from mice and cell studies, including models of metabolic syndrome, heart failure and kidney aging. No human trial results have been published. Anti-doping laboratories have published methods for detecting it.

name: BAM-15

angle.text: BAM15 is traded online as a "safer DNP", with users hoping to raise calorie burn and shed fat for a leaner look. The evidence is from mouse studies showing fat loss; human effects have not been tested.

summary: A mitochondrial uncoupler that burns fat in mice and is traded online as a 'safer DNP'; no human data exist.
note: No human safety data; uncoupling class has documented toxicity.
currentQuick:
BAM15 is an experimental compound that makes mitochondria burn fuel as heat. In mice it cut fat mass and improved blood sugar.
Forum users discuss it as an alternative to DNP, but no human trials have been published.
How it works: It carries protons across the mitochondrial membrane, uncoupling food oxidation from ATP production and raising energy expenditure.
Risks and caveats: Human safety is unstudied. Uncouplers as a class can cause overheating, and DNP has been linked to fatal poisonings. BAM15 is not approved.
deepLead:
BAM15 is an experimental mitochondrial uncoupler, a small molecule that lets protons leak across the inner mitochondrial membrane so that nutrient oxidation produces heat rather than ATP. It was identified in a 2014 screen as an uncoupler that did not depolarize the plasma membrane.
In mice fed a high-fat diet, oral BAM15 reduced body fat and improved insulin sensitivity without changing food intake in studies reported in 2020. Wikipedia notes no human trials. It is discussed in fat-loss communities as a possible alternative to the older uncoupler DNP; no published human data support its use for that purpose.

name: Adipotide

angle.text: Adipotide is discussed in fat-loss forums as a peptide that targets the blood supply of fat tissue to shrink it. Its weight loss was shown in obese monkeys, while human data are absent and development stopped.

summary: Experimental fat-vessel-targeting peptide that cut weight in monkeys; no human data and development stopped.
note: Animal data only; clinical development reported discontinued.
currentQuick:
Adipotide is an experimental peptide designed to destroy the blood vessels that feed white fat. Obese monkeys lost weight in a 2011 study.
A later comment suggested reduced eating could explain part of the effect. No human results exist.
How it works: It binds prohibitin on fat blood vessels and triggers cell death in them, starving fat tissue.
Risks and caveats: Human safety is unknown, and it is not approved. Clinical development was reported discontinued.
deepLead:
Adipotide (also called prohibitin-targeting peptide 1, FTPP or TP01) is an experimental peptidomimetic designed to bind prohibitin and annexin A2 on the blood vessels feeding white fat, inducing the death of those vessels and, in turn, fat tissue.
In a 2011 study in obese rhesus monkeys, treatment reduced body weight and improved insulin resistance. A 2012 published comment proposed the weight loss might instead reflect reduced food intake. Wikipedia lists its status as investigational, with clinical development discontinued as of 2019. No human trial results are published.

name: Fenfluramine

angle.text: Fenfluramine was a widely used prescription appetite suppressant, often combined with phentermine as fen-phen, and is cited in diet-drug history as a strong weight-loss option. Its weight-loss effect was studied in trials, and it was withdrawn in 1997; it is now an epilepsy medicine.

summary: Former prescription diet drug withdrawn in 1997 over heart valve harm; now a restricted epilepsy medicine.
note: Boxed warning for valvular heart disease and pulmonary hypertension.
currentQuick:
Fenfluramine was a widely prescribed appetite suppressant, best known in the fen-phen combination, until it was withdrawn from the US market in 1997 after reports of heart valve disease.
A low-dose form is now sold as Fintepla for certain childhood epilepsies, not for weight loss.
How it works: It releases serotonin and acts at 5-HT2 receptors, which reduces appetite; how it prevents seizures is not known.
Risks and caveats: The label carries a boxed warning for valvular heart disease and pulmonary arterial hypertension, and use requires echocardiogram monitoring through a restricted program.
deepLead:
Fenfluramine is an amphetamine-derived serotonin-releasing drug. Introduced in France in 1963 and approved in the United States in 1973 as an appetite suppressant (brand name Pondimin), it was widely used for weight loss, often with phentermine in the combination known as fen-phen.
It was withdrawn from the US market in 1997 after reports of heart valve disease and pulmonary hypertension in users. Fenfluramine was reintroduced at lower doses as Fintepla, approved by the FDA in 2020 for seizures in Dravet syndrome and later Lennox-Gastaut syndrome, under a restricted program with echocardiogram monitoring.

name: Ephedrine/caffeine (ECA stack)

angle.text: The ECA stack is a classic cutting aid in bodybuilding circles, used to boost energy and fat loss while dieting for a leaner, more defined physique. Trials have found modest fat-loss effects, mostly alongside diet and exercise.

summary: A classic ephedrine, caffeine and aspirin cutting stack with modest reported fat-loss effects and a long regulatory history.
note: Ephedrine-alkaloid supplements are banned in the US; cardiovascular events have been reported.
currentQuick:
ECA combines ephedrine, caffeine and aspirin. It is used in bodybuilding and physique communities as a cutting aid for appetite suppression and energy.
A 2021 systematic review summarized on Wikipedia reported about 2 kg more weight loss than placebo over 4 to 24 weeks.
How it works: Ephedrine is a sympathomimetic stimulant; caffeine has been reported to act synergistically with it.
Risks and caveats: Reported effects include insomnia, anxiety, high blood pressure, fast heart rate, stroke and heart attack. The FDA banned ephedrine-alkaloid supplements in 2004; legal status varies elsewhere.
deepLead:
The ECA stack is a combination of ephedrine, caffeine and aspirin used as a fat-loss and energy aid, particularly in bodybuilding and physique-cutting circles. Ephedrine is a sympathomimetic stimulant derived from or chemically identical to the alkaloids of the ephedra plant, and caffeine is thought to amplify its effects.
A 2021 systematic review summarized on Wikipedia reported that ephedrine, with or without caffeine, taken for roughly 4 to 24 weeks was associated with about 2 kg more weight loss than placebo, with no statistically significant blood pressure difference in that review. Ephedrine is also associated with insomnia, anxiety, raised blood pressure, fast heart rate, and, in serious cases, stroke and heart attack.
In the United States, the FDA banned ephedrine-alkaloid dietary supplements marketed for purposes other than traditional uses in 2004, and a federal appeals court upheld that rule in 2006. Users on looksmax.org have written ECA guides that frame it as a cutting aid to be paired with exercise and caution against it for people with heart problems.

name: Zenagamtide

angle.text: Zenagamtide (amycretin) is a not-yet-approved dual GLP-1/amylin drug followed closely in fat-loss circles because early trials reported large weight-loss figures. Evidence is from early-stage trials in obesity; its use for cosmetic leanness has not been studied.

summary: Novo Nordisk's investigational GLP-1 plus amylin dual agonist, with large weight-loss figures in early trials and no approval yet.
note: Not approved; reported gastrointestinal side effects.
currentQuick:
Zenagamtide is the name for amycretin, a single molecule that activates GLP-1 and amylin receptors. Novo Nordisk is developing weekly injectable and daily oral forms for obesity and diabetes.
Early trials were published in the Lancet in 2025; an AI-generated source reports up to about 24 percent weight loss at 36 weeks in the injectable trial.
How it works: It combines GLP-1 and amylin receptor activity in one peptide, acting on appetite, satiety and gastric emptying.
Risks and caveats: Gastrointestinal effects were the most common reported adverse events. It is investigational and not approved.
deepLead:
Zenagamtide, better known by the name amycretin, is an investigational once-weekly injectable and daily oral drug from Novo Nordisk that activates both the GLP-1 and amylin receptors within a single peptide molecule. It is being developed for obesity and type 2 diabetes and is not approved.
In a phase 1b/2a trial of 125 adults with overweight or obesity running up to 36 weeks, subcutaneous amycretin was studied for safety, tolerability and weight effects. Grokipedia, an AI-generated source, reports a mean weight loss of 24.3 percent at the 60 mg weekly dose and gastrointestinal adverse events as the most common effects. Phase 3 programs were reported to be planned or starting.

name: Enicepatide

angle.text: Enicepatide is Roche's investigational weekly GLP-1/GIP dual agonist, watched by weight-loss followers as a possible rival to tirzepatide. It is in phase 3 trials for obesity; appearance-focused use has not been studied.

summary: Roche's weekly GLP-1/GIP dual agonist, now in phase 3 and headed for a tirzepatide head-to-head.
note: Investigational; not approved.
currentQuick:
Enicepatide is a weekly injectable that activates GLP-1 and GIP receptors, from Roche. It is in phase 3 for obesity and type 2 diabetes.
Wikipedia cites 18.8 percent placebo-adjusted weight loss at 24 weeks in a trial.
How it works: A signal-biased dual agonist of GLP-1 and GIP receptors with minimal beta-arrestin coupling.
Risks and caveats: Investigational and unapproved; published safety information is limited in available sources.
deepLead:
Enicepatide (CT-388, RO7795068) is an investigational once-weekly injectable drug that activates the GLP-1 and GIP receptors, developed by Roche for obesity and type 2 diabetes. It is described as signal-biased, meaning it shows minimal beta-arrestin coupling at either receptor.
Wikipedia cites a 24-week trial with 18.8 percent placebo-adjusted weight loss. Roche has registered phase 3 trials in people with obesity, with and without type 2 diabetes, including a comparison with tirzepatide. It is not approved.

name: CT-996

angle.text: CT-996 is an experimental oral GLP-1 pill from Roche, followed by fat-loss communities interested in a non-injectable alternative to semaglutide-type drugs. It has registered phase 2 trials and no published results, so its weight-loss effect is untested.

summary: Roche's experimental oral GLP-1 pill, with registered phase 2 trials and no results seen yet.
note: Investigational; no published efficacy data found.
currentQuick:
CT-996 (tifeglipron) is an experimental oral GLP-1 agonist from Roche for obesity and type 2 diabetes.
Phase 2 trials are registered; results were not found.
How it works: A small-molecule agonist of the GLP-1 receptor taken by mouth, rather than a peptide injection.
Risks and caveats: No published safety or efficacy data were found. Not approved.
deepLead:
CT-996 is an investigational oral small-molecule GLP-1 receptor agonist from Roche, also registered under the code RO7795081 and the name tifeglipron. Small-molecule oral GLP-1 agonists are a class designed to avoid the injection requirement of peptide drugs.
Published results for CT-996 were not found; the evidence is limited to clinical trial registrations covering phase 1 and phase 2 studies.

name: Petrelintide

angle.text: Petrelintide is a weekly amylin analogue from Zealand and Roche, discussed in fat-loss circles as part of the next wave of obesity drugs beyond GLP-1. It is in phase 3 for weight management; its appearance effects specifically have not been studied.

summary: A weekly amylin-analogue obesity drug from Zealand and Roche, now in phase 3.
note: Investigational; not approved.
currentQuick:
Petrelintide is a weekly injectable amylin analogue from Zealand Pharma, partnered with Roche. It targets satiety rather than GLP-1 pathways.
A phase 1b trial reported 8.6 percent weight loss over 16 weeks; phase 2 results were published in 2026.
How it works: It mimics amylin, a hormone that signals fullness after meals.
Risks and caveats: Investigational; safety data are in phase 1 and 2 publications. Not approved.
deepLead:
Petrelintide (ZP8396) is an investigational once-weekly amylin analogue discovered by Zealand Pharma for weight management. In March 2025 Roche entered a collaboration with Zealand to co-develop and co-commercialise it, alone and in combination with CT-388 (enicepatide).
A phase 1b trial reported in June 2024 weight loss of 8.6 percent over 16 weeks. A phase 2 trial, ZUPREME 1, has been published in The Lancet Diabetes & Endocrinology, and phase 3 trials have begun recruiting. It is not approved.

name: Eloralintide

angle.text: Eloralintide is Lilly's weekly amylin agonist, followed by fat-loss communities because phase 2 trials reported roughly 9 to 20 percent weight loss at 48 weeks. It is unapproved, and use for cosmetic leanness has not been studied.

summary: Lilly's weekly amylin agonist, with reported weight loss of roughly 9 to 20 percent at 48 weeks in phase 2.
note: Investigational; GI side effects reported.
currentQuick:
Eloralintide is a weekly injectable amylin agonist from Eli Lilly. Phase 2 results appeared in the Lancet in 2025 and phase 3 trials are underway.
An AI-generated source reports 9.5 to 20.1 percent weight loss at 48 weeks.
How it works: It selectively activates the amylin receptor, promoting fullness and slowing stomach emptying.
Risks and caveats: Nausea and other gastrointestinal effects were most common. Not approved.
deepLead:
Eloralintide (LY3841136) is an investigational once-weekly selective amylin receptor agonist from Eli Lilly for obesity. It is not approved.
A 48-week phase 2 trial in adults with obesity or overweight and a comorbidity was published in The Lancet in 2025. Grokipedia, an AI-generated source, reports weight loss ranging from 9.5 percent at the lowest dose to 20.1 percent at the highest, versus 0.4 percent with placebo, with nausea and other gastrointestinal effects the most common adverse events. Lilly began phase 3 trials in December 2025.

name: Maridebart cafraglutide

angle.text: MariTide is Amgen's monthly injection discussed in fat-loss circles for its less frequent dosing and roughly 12-16% weight loss at a year in phase 2. It is in phase 3, and appearance-focused outcomes have not been studied.

summary: Amgen's monthly GLP-1 agonist / GIP-blocker injection, still in phase 3, with roughly 12-16% weight loss at a year in phase 2.
note: Investigational and not approved; only available inside clinical trials.
currentQuick:
Maridebart cafraglutide (MariTide) is an experimental injectable obesity drug from Amgen. It is designed to be given monthly or less often, unlike weekly semaglutide or tirzepatide.
In a phase 2 trial of 592 adults, average weight loss at 52 weeks was 12.3% to 16.2% in people with obesity, versus 2.5% on placebo. Large phase 3 trials are under way.
How it works: It pairs an antibody that blocks the GIP receptor with GLP-1 peptides that activate the GLP-1 receptor. The antibody backbone extends its time in the body, supporting infrequent dosing.
Risks and caveats: Nausea, vomiting and other gastrointestinal events were common in phase 2, and less frequent with gradual dose escalation. No unexpected safety signals were reported. It is not approved anywhere, and long-term safety data are still being collected.
deepLead:
Maridebart cafraglutide, also known as MariTide and formerly AMG 133, is an investigational drug developed by Amgen for obesity and related conditions. It is a long-acting antibody-peptide conjugate: a fully human antibody that blocks the GIP receptor, linked to GLP-1 analogue peptides that activate the GLP-1 receptor. 
In a phase 2 randomised, placebo-controlled trial published in the New England Journal of Medicine, people with obesity who received the drug by subcutaneous injection every 4 weeks or less often lost between 12.3% and 16.2% of body weight at 52 weeks (treatment-policy estimand), compared with 2.5% on placebo. Gastrointestinal adverse events were common but less frequent with dose escalation and a lower starting dose, and the investigators reported no unexpected safety signals. 
As of late 2026 the drug is not approved by any regulator. It is in phase 3 development under Amgen's MARITIME programme, with registered trials in obesity, type 2 diabetes, heart failure, sleep apnoea and cardiovascular outcomes.  It is discussed in appearance-focused communities mainly as one of the next-generation injectable weight-loss drugs, because of its monthly or less frequent dosing.

name: Aleniglipron

angle.text: Aleniglipron is an experimental once-daily GLP-1 pill that fat-loss followers watch as a non-injectable option, with phase 2b trials showing about 8-11% placebo-adjusted weight loss over 36 weeks. Its use for cosmetic leanness has not been studied.

summary: An experimental once-daily GLP-1 pill that cut weight by about 8-11% (placebo-adjusted) over 36 weeks in phase 2b.
note: Investigational and not approved; phase 3 under way.
currentQuick:
Aleniglipron is an experimental oral GLP-1 agonist for obesity. It is a once-daily small-molecule pill rather than an injectable peptide.
In a 36-week phase 2b trial of 230 adults, placebo-adjusted weight loss ranged from 8.2% to 11.3% depending on dose. Phase 3 trials started in 2026.
How it works: It activates the GLP-1 receptor, the pathway used by semaglutide and similar drugs that reduces appetite and food intake. Being a non-peptide, it can be taken by mouth.
Risks and caveats: Gastrointestinal events were the main adverse effects and were mostly mild to moderate; 10.4% of drug-arm participants stopped treatment for treatment-related reasons, and no drug-induced liver injury was reported. It is not approved and long-term data are lacking.
deepLead:
Aleniglipron (development code GSBR-1290) is an investigational oral, small-molecule glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonist being developed for obesity and overweight. Unlike injectable peptide GLP-1 drugs such as semaglutide, it is a non-peptide pill taken once daily. 
In the ACCESS phase 2b trial, 230 adults with obesity or overweight received aleniglipron or placebo for 36 weeks. Placebo-adjusted weight change was -8.2%, -9.8% and -11.3% at the 45, 90 and 120 mg arms respectively. Gastrointestinal events were generally mild to moderate, and treatment-related discontinuations were 10.4% across drug arms, with no drug-induced liver injury reported. 
The drug is not approved. Phase 3 trials (ACCOMPLISH-1 and ACCOMPLISH-2) began registering participants in 2026.
